title: Memory management and virtual memory
subtitle: Programs think they own a huge private address space. The OS and the MMU make that true with pages, page tables, and a policy for what to throw out. This chapter goes from base registers to demand paging, with the arithmetic examiners ask for.

sections.title: Why memory needs managing
sections.body:
A CPU can run only what is in main memory, and main memory is shared by the OS and by every running process. The memory manager has four jobs. Relocation: a program cannot know in advance where in RAM it will be loaded, so its addresses must be translated. Protection: one process must not read or write another’s memory, nor the kernel’s. Sharing: sometimes processes should share (library code, shared memory). Organisation: memory must be used efficiently, with little wasted and the ability to run programs larger than RAM.

The key idea behind every scheme is the distinction between a logical (virtual) address — the address the program generates — and a physical address — the actual location in RAM. The hardware memory-management unit (MMU) translates one into the other on every memory reference. Because translation happens at run time, the OS can move a program in memory, give it non-contiguous pieces, and even keep only part of it resident. “Address binding” can happen at compile time (absolute code, rare), load time (relocatable code fixed when loaded) or, in modern systems, execution time (the MMU).

The simplest MMU is a pair of registers: base and limit. Every logical address is compared with the limit (a protection check) and added to the base to give the physical address. Switching processes means loading different base/limit values — nothing else is needed to isolate them.

worked.why: A process has base = 14000 and limit = 3000. The program generates logical address 2500 and then 3200. Translate each.
2500 is below the limit 3000, so it is legal: physical = 14000 + 2500.
3200 ≥ 3000 exceeds the limit: the hardware traps to the OS (addressing error) — the process tried to leave its region.

questions.prompt: At which time does a system with an MMU bind logical addresses to physical addresses?

choices.text: At compile time only.
At execution time, on every reference.
At boot time.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That would fix the program’s location forever.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Run-time binding is what allows the OS to relocate a process while it runs.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Boot has nothing to do with each program’s addresses.

problems.prompt: Base = 40000, limit = 12000. For logical addresses 0, 11999 and 12000, give the physical address or say it traps.
problems.answer: 0 → 40000. 11999 → 51999. 12000 equals the limit, so it is outside the legal range 0…11999 → trap.

sections.title: Contiguous allocation and fragmentation
sections.body:
The simplest scheme gives each process one contiguous block of physical memory. Early systems cut memory into fixed partitions, which wastes the unused part of each partition (internal fragmentation). Later systems use variable partitions: the OS keeps a list of free holes and, for each request, chooses one. First fit takes the first hole big enough (fast); best fit takes the smallest hole that fits (leaves the smallest leftover, but scans the whole list and tends to create tiny useless slivers); worst fit takes the largest (leaves a big remainder, but destroys the large holes). Simulation studies show first fit and best fit beat worst fit in storage use, with first fit usually faster.

Whatever is left over is too small to use — external fragmentation. Statistically, for first fit about one third of memory ends up unusable (the “50 % rule”: for every N allocated blocks about N/2 are lost to fragmentation). Compaction squeezes all the holes into one by moving processes, but it needs run-time relocation and costs a great deal of copying. Paging, next, removes the problem at its root. Run the three cards: the same requests are placed very differently.

questions.prompt: Free holes are 100, 500, 200, 300, 600 KB. Which policy can place all four requests 212, 417, 112, 426?

choices.text: Best fit — the others strand memory and leave 426 unplaced.
First fit.
Worst fit.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: First fit and worst fit carve big holes into pieces that no longer fit 426; best fit keeps the large holes whole (result: 212→B4 417→B2 112→B3 426→B5).

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: It leaves 1 request unplaced: 426 KB has no hole left once 212 and 112 have split the 500 KB block.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: It also fails on 426 KB (1 unplaced) because it keeps shaving the largest hole.

questions.prompt: Which kind of fragmentation do fixed-size partitions suffer from?

choices.text: External fragmentation only.
Internal fragmentation: space wasted inside each allocated partition.
Neither.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That arises with variable partitions.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A 100 KB process in a 150 KB partition wastes 50 KB that nobody else can use.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Fixed partitions waste space inside the partition.

problems.prompt: Holes of 10, 4, 20, 18, 7, 9, 12 and 15 KB (in this order). Place a request of 12 KB, then 10 KB, then 9 KB with first fit. Which holes are used?
problems.answer: 12 KB → first hole that fits is 20 (leaves 8). 10 KB → the 10 KB hole (leaves 0). 9 KB → first hole ≥ 9 in order is now 18 (the 20 became 8, the 4 and 7 are too small, 8 is too small) → 18 (leaves 9). Holes used: 20, 10, 18.

sections.title: Paging
sections.body:
Paging cuts the virtual address space into fixed-size pages and physical memory into same-size frames. Any page can go in any frame, so external fragmentation disappears; only the last page of a process wastes part of a frame (internal fragmentation, on average half a page). A per-process page table maps page number → frame number. A virtual address of m bits with page size 2n splits into a page number (the top m − n bits) and an offset (the low n bits); the offset passes through unchanged because pages and frames are the same size.

With 4 KB pages (n = 12), the address 0x3A7C has page number 3 and offset 0xA7C; if page 3 lives in frame 9, the physical address is 9·4096 + 0xA7C. The page table entry also carries valid (is the page in memory?), protection (read/write/execute), dirty (modified?) and referenced bits — the hooks for protection and for replacement.

Where does the page table live? In main memory — which means each reference costs two memory accesses: one for the page-table entry, one for the data. To avoid the doubling, the MMU has a small, fast associative cache of recent translations, the TLB (translation look-aside buffer). A TLB hit gives the frame in one fast step; a miss walks the table and loads the entry. Because programs show locality, hit ratios of 98–99 % are normal. The effective access time is a weighted average, worked below and tabulated in the figure.

worked.why: 4 KB pages → 12 offset bits. Virtual address 0x3A7C: page number = 0x3A7C >> 12 = 3, offset = 0xA7C.
If page 3 is in frame 9, the physical address is frame × 4096 + offset = 36864 + 2684.
Effective access time with TLB hit ratio h = 0.9, TLB lookup 10 ns, memory access 100 ns: a hit costs 10 + 100; a miss costs 10 + 100 (page table) + 100 (data).

questions.prompt: During translation, what happens to the offset bits?

choices.text: They are multiplied by the frame number.
They pass through unchanged — only the page number is replaced by a frame number.
They are looked up in the page table.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Nothing is multiplied; the frame number is shifted into the high bits.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Pages and frames are the same size, so a byte keeps its position inside the page.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: The page table is indexed by page number only.

questions.prompt: Why does a TLB make paging practical?

choices.text: It stores the program’s data.
It makes the pages bigger.
It caches recent page→frame translations, so most references avoid the extra memory access for the page table.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: The TLB holds translations only, not data.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Page size is set by the architecture, not the TLB.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Locality of reference gives hit ratios near 99 %.

questions.prompt: A process needs 72,766 bytes and the page size is 2,048 bytes. How much is lost to internal fragmentation?

choices.text: 962 bytes — it needs 36 pages (73,728 bytes) and 36 × 2,048 − 72,766 = 962.
0 bytes, because paging has no fragmentation.
2,048 bytes.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: 72,766 / 2,048 = 35.53, so 35 full pages plus a partly filled 36th; the unused tail of the last page is internal fragmentation.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Paging removes external fragmentation, not internal.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: That is a whole extra page, but the last page is partly used.

figures.caption: Figure 4.3.1 — address translation
figures.note: A TLB hit skips the page-table walk.

figures.caption: Figure 4.3.2 — paging with a TLB
figures.note: TLB lookup 10 ns, memory 100 ns. Without a TLB every access costs 200 ns; a 98 % hit ratio gets within 12 % of the ideal 100 ns.

problems.prompt: A 32-bit system uses 4 KB pages. Give the page number and offset of address 0x00403A7C, and the number of pages in the address space.
problems.answer: Offset = low 12 bits = 0xA7C. Page number = 0x00403A7C >> 12 = 0x00403 = 1027. The address space has 2³² / 2¹² = 2²⁰ = 1,048,576 pages.

problems.prompt: Memory access takes 80 ns and the TLB lookup 5 ns. What hit ratio is needed for an effective access time of at most 95 ns?

sections.title: Page-table size: multilevel and inverted tables
sections.body:
A flat page table can be enormous. With 32-bit addresses and 4 KB pages there are 2²⁰ pages; at 4 bytes per entry the table is 4 MB per process, most of it describing addresses the process never uses. On a 64-bit machine a flat table is impossible. The standard cure is a hierarchical (multilevel) page table: page the page table itself. A 32-bit address is split 10 + 10 + 12: the first 10 bits index an outer table whose entries point to inner tables, the next 10 bits index the inner table, and the last 12 are the offset. Inner tables for unused regions simply do not exist, so a small process uses a handful of tables. The price is more memory accesses per translation on a TLB miss (one per level), which the TLB hides.

An alternative is the inverted page table: one entry per physical frame, recording which (process, page) occupies it. Its size depends on RAM, not on address-space size, which suits 64-bit machines, but looking up a page means searching the table — made fast with a hash on (pid, page number). Sharing pages between processes is harder in this scheme.

worked.why: 32-bit addresses, 4 KB pages, 4-byte entries. Size of a flat page table?
Two-level: a 10-bit outer index gives 1024 inner tables, each of 1024 entries × 4 B = 4 KB — exactly one page, which is why 10 + 10 + 12 is the classic split.

questions.prompt: Why is a two-level page table smaller than a flat one for a typical process?

choices.text: Inner tables are created only for the parts of the address space actually in use.
Because it uses larger pages.
Because it stores no frame numbers.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The outer table is small, and most outer entries are empty.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: The page size is unchanged.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: It stores frame numbers; it just stores far fewer entries.

questions.prompt: What is the main trade-off of an inverted page table?

choices.text: It is bigger than a flat table.
Memory use is small (one entry per frame) but finding a page requires a search or hash.
It does not need a TLB.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: It is much smaller for large address spaces.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Table size follows physical memory, not the virtual address space.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: The TLB is still needed to avoid the lookup cost.

problems.prompt: A 32-bit address space uses 4 KB pages and a two-level page table with 10 bits at each level. How many entries does the outer table have, and how many bytes is one inner table with 4-byte entries?
problems.answer: Outer table: 2¹⁰ = 1024 entries. Inner table: 1024 × 4 B = 4096 bytes (one page).

sections.title: Segmentation
sections.body:
Paging splits memory by size; segmentation divides a program by meaning — code, data, stack, each library — as a programmer thinks of it. An address is a pair (segment, offset); a segment table holds each segment’s base and limit, and an offset beyond the limit is a protection fault. Segments are visible to the programmer and variable-sized, so they bring back external fragmentation and a more complicated allocation problem, but they make protection and sharing natural: a code segment can be marked read-only and shared by many processes, a stack segment can grow independently.

Real systems combine both ideas. Intel’s early x86 used segmentation; modern 64-bit systems use a flat model with paging. A paged segment scheme splits each segment into pages, so segments give meaningful protection while pages give fixed-size allocation.

worked.why: Segment table: segment 2 has base 4300 and limit 400. Translate (2, 100).
Check the offset against the limit.

questions.prompt: Segment 2 has base 4300 and limit 400. What happens for (2, 500)?

choices.text: Physical address 4800.
It wraps around to offset 100.
A protection fault — the offset exceeds the limit.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Adding base and offset without checking the limit is the bug segmentation prevents.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: There is no wrap-around; out-of-range is an error.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The limit register exists precisely to stop a program reaching beyond its own segment.

questions.prompt: Which is a real advantage of segmentation over pure paging?

choices.text: Segments match the program’s logical structure, so protection and sharing (e.g. a read-only code segment) are natural.
It eliminates all fragmentation.
It needs no translation hardware.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Pages are invisible to the programmer and carry no meaning.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Segmentation suffers external fragmentation.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: It needs a segment table and limit checks.

problems.prompt: A segment table: seg 0 (base 1400, limit 1000), seg 1 (base 6300, limit 400), seg 2 (base 4300, limit 400). Translate (0, 999), (1, 400) and (2, 53).

sections.title: Virtual memory and demand paging
sections.body:
Why load a whole program when most of it — error handlers, rarely used features — never runs? Virtual memory separates the programmer’s view of memory from the physical reality: a program may be larger than RAM because only the pages actually in use need be resident, the rest living on disk (the swap area or the executable itself). With demand paging a page is brought in only when it is first referenced. Each page-table entry has a valid bit; if it is clear, the reference triggers a page fault.

Handling a page fault takes a dozen steps, and the figure walks through them: the MMU traps to the OS; the OS checks that the reference is legal (otherwise it kills the process); it finds a free frame (or evicts one); it schedules a disk read and switches to another process while waiting; when the read completes it updates the page table and ready queue; finally it restarts the faulting instruction, which now succeeds. The instruction is restarted from scratch, which is why the hardware must be able to undo a half-finished instruction.

A fault costs milliseconds against nanoseconds for a normal access — a factor of tens of thousands — so even a tiny fault rate hurts. The effective access time is EAT = (1 − p)·m + p·F, where p is the fault probability, m the memory access time and F the fault service time. The worked example turns this into a requirement on p.

worked.why: Memory access m = 200 ns; a page fault takes F = 8 ms = 8,000,000 ns. What fault probability keeps the slowdown below 10 %?
So p must be below about one fault in 400,000 references.

choices.text: It loads the whole program before it starts.
It loads a page into memory only when the process first references it.
It compresses pages on disk.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That is the opposite: pure demand paging starts with no pages resident.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Pages never used never occupy a frame.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Compression is a separate technique.

questions.prompt: Why must the page-fault rate be extremely small?

choices.text: Because faults corrupt data.
A fault costs milliseconds while a normal access costs nanoseconds — about 10⁴–10⁵ times more.
Because the disk fills up.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Faults are normal and safe; the issue is time.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Even 1 fault in 1000 accesses would slow the program dramatically.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Faults do not fill the disk.

figures.caption: Figure 4.6.1 — servicing a page fault
figures.note: While the disk works, the OS runs some other process.
figures.script:
diagram("mode: sequence
[Process] as p
[MMU] as m
[OS] as o
[Disk] as d
p -> m : reference page 7 (valid bit = 0)
m -> o : page-fault trap
o -> o : legal reference? pick a free frame
o -> d : read page 7 into frame 12
d -> o : interrupt: transfer done
o -> m : update page table, valid = 1
o -> p : restart the faulting instruction
p -> m : reference succeeds");

problems.prompt: m = 100 ns, F = 10 ms. If the fault rate is 1 per 10,000 references, what is the effective access time?
problems.answer: p = 10⁻⁴. EAT = (1 − p)(100) + p(10,000,000) = 99.99 + 1000 = ≈ 1100 ns — eleven times slower than a fault-free system.

sections.title: Page replacement
sections.body:
If a fault occurs and no frame is free, the OS must evict a page. The goal of every policy is to evict the page that will be needed furthest in the future. FIFO evicts the oldest resident page — trivially cheap, but it may throw out a heavily used page just because it arrived early. LRU evicts the least recently used page, using the past as a predictor of the future (locality of reference). The unreachable optimal policy evicts the page needed furthest ahead; it needs the future so it cannot be built, but it is the yardstick every algorithm is measured against. LFU evicts the least frequently used page.

Exact LRU is expensive (a timestamp or a stack update on every reference), so real kernels approximate it. The second-chance (clock) algorithm keeps pages in a circular list with a reference bit: the hand sweeps; a page with bit 1 gets the bit cleared and a second chance, a page with bit 0 is evicted. Enhanced versions consider the dirty bit too, preferring clean pages (no write-back needed). Pages are also evicted in the background so a free frame is waiting at fault time.

On the textbook reference string with 3 frames: FIFO = 15 faults, LRU = 12, optimal = 9 of 20 references. The cards animate each: red marks a fault, green a hit.

questions.prompt: Why does LRU usually beat FIFO?

choices.text: LRU is cheaper to implement.
Programs show locality: a page used recently is likely to be used again soon, while an old page may still be hot.
LRU never faults more than FIFO.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: The opposite: exact LRU needs bookkeeping on every reference.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: FIFO only knows age of loading; LRU tracks use, which is what predicts the future.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Not a theorem; it tends to win on real programs, not on every string.

questions.prompt: In the clock (second-chance) algorithm, what happens to a page whose reference bit is 1 when the hand reaches it?

choices.text: The bit is cleared and the page is spared; the hand moves on.
It is evicted immediately.
It is written to disk.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Only a page found with bit 0 is evicted, so recently used pages survive.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: That is what happens to a page with bit 0.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Writing back depends on the dirty bit, not the reference bit.

questions.prompt: Why can the optimal policy not be implemented in a real OS?

choices.text: It needs too much memory.
It requires knowledge of future references.
It evicts the wrong page.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: The memory is trivial; the future knowledge is impossible.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It is used only as a benchmark to judge other algorithms.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: It evicts exactly the right page, which is why it is optimal.

problems.prompt: Reference string 7 0 1 2 0 3 0 4 2 3 0 3 2 1 2 0 1 7 0 1 with 3 frames: count faults for FIFO, LRU and optimal.

sections.title: Belady's anomaly
sections.body:
More frames should mean fewer faults — but not for FIFO. On the string 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5, three frames give 9 faults and four frames give 10: Belady's anomaly. It happens because FIFO’s resident set with n frames is not always a subset of its resident set with n + 1 frames, so the extra frame can change which pages are present at the wrong moment. Algorithms for which the set of pages in memory with n frames is always a subset of that with n + 1 frames — LRU and optimal — are called stack algorithms and cannot show the anomaly.

Run both cards below and compare the fault counts. The lesson is subtle: the anomaly is rare in practice, but it destroys the intuition that adding memory can only help, and it is the standard exam question on why FIFO is a poor policy.

questions.prompt: FIFO with 4 frames faults more than with 3 on the same string. What does this show?

choices.text: The simulator has a bug.
Four frames is too many for this string.
Adding memory does not always help FIFO — Belady's anomaly.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: It is a real, classic result reproduced exactly by the textbook string.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: More frames can never be “too many”; the policy is at fault.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: FIFO's eviction order ignores use, so a larger memory can shift which pages are resident at the wrong moment (9 → 10 faults).

questions.prompt: Why can LRU never show Belady’s anomaly?

choices.text: It never evicts any page.
It is a stack algorithm: the pages resident with n frames are always a subset of those with n + 1 frames.
It uses a larger page size.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: It evicts when needed, but by recency.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: So more frames can only keep more of the useful pages.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Page size is unrelated.

sections.title: Frame allocation and thrashing
sections.body:
With several processes, how many frames should each get? Equal allocation gives m/n frames to each of n processes; proportional allocation gives each a share proportional to its size. Replacement can be local (a process evicts only its own pages — predictable but may starve) or global (any frame may be taken — better throughput but one process can hurt another).

Thrashing is the failure mode. A process needs a minimum number of frames to make progress — its working set, the pages it has referenced in the last Δ references. If it has fewer frames than its working set, it faults continually; the processes queue at the disk; the CPU, seeing low utilisation, admits more processes (the long-term scheduler thinks it should raise multiprogramming), which steal even more frames — a vicious circle in which utilisation collapses. The cure is to measure the working sets (or the page-fault frequency) and, when the total demand exceeds memory, to suspend some processes entirely rather than slow all of them.

worked.why: Two processes of sizes 10 pages and 127 pages share 62 frames. Proportional allocation gives each frame share: s₁ = 10, s₂ = 127, S = 137.

questions.prompt: A system shows low CPU utilisation and a saturated paging disk. What is the correct response?

choices.text: Add more processes to keep the CPU busy.
Make the time quantum shorter.
Reduce the degree of multiprogramming (suspend processes) so the remaining ones fit their working sets.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That is exactly the mistake that deepens thrashing.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: The quantum does not address the lack of frames.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Adding more processes would make thrashing worse.

questions.prompt: What is a process’s working set?

choices.text: All the pages of its program.
The pages on disk.
The set of pages it has referenced in the most recent window of Δ references.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That is its size, not its current need.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: The working set is about pages in active use.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: If it fits in memory, the process runs smoothly; if not, it faults constantly.

problems.prompt: Explain how a long-term scheduler that watches only CPU utilisation can make thrashing worse.
problems.answer: Thrashing makes CPU utilisation fall (everything waits on the disk). A scheduler that reacts to low utilisation by admitting more processes takes frames away from those already running, making their faults worse and utilisation lower still. The scheduler must also watch the fault rate or working-set sizes.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Logical addresses are translated to physical ones by the MMU on every reference; base/limit is the simplest scheme.
  • Contiguous allocation suffers external fragmentation (first/best/worst fit); paging removes it, with a page table mapping page → frame and the offset unchanged.
  • The TLB hides the page-table cost: EAT = h(t + m) + (1 − h)(t + 2m). Multilevel and inverted tables shrink the table.
  • Segmentation matches program structure; real systems combine segments and pages.
  • Demand paging loads on first reference; EAT = (1 − p)m + pF, so p must be tiny.
  • Optimal ≤ LRU ≲ FIFO on real programs; FIFO can even get worse with more frames (Belady); clock approximates LRU.
  • Thrashing = fewer frames than the working set; cure by suspending processes.
